metadata.title: ChatGPT: The brightest student in the class

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study used a small, recruited sample of Spanish secondary-school students and Spanish language teachers to compare human-written and ChatGPT-generated summaries. No complex survey design or ILSA sampling weights are described, and the analysis is based on teacher ratings using a rubric rather than population-representative estimation. Because the design is an experimental-style classroom task with purposive recruitment across Spanish regions, there is no stated use of sampling weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife). The weighting strategy is therefore not applicable to this dataset; results should be interpreted as evidence about scoring differences in this study context rather than national inference.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values are not applicable because the dependent variables are rubric-based teacher ratings of a single summary task (content and style scores), not PV-based cognitive achievement scores from PISA. The paper also does not report a missing-data handling strategy (e.g., how incomplete teacher returns or missing rubric components were treated), which is a reporting gap for transparency, even though the study appears to exclude some teacher responses during recruitment.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic sample comprised 30 Spanish students aged 149e16 (16 females, 14 males) recruited from five secondary school centers. Students wrote a summary of a PISA 2009 reading comprehension text (385 words) in no more than 125 words. Teachers were selected from five Spanish regions; 51 teachers were initially approached and 21 corrections were rejected (5 due to lack of informed consent and 16 to create a homogeneous sample across teacher sex, age, and experience), yielding 30 teachers (16 women, 14 men) who corrected the camouflaged summaries using a provided rubric.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2009 reading comprehension text (summary task), Spain (secondary students, 149e16)
main_findings.performance_metrics: No ML metrics reported. Descriptive differences: all style differences > 3 points. Inferential tests: gender effect not significant (t-test, p > 0.05; Table 3: p=0.160). Teacher age effect significant (one-factor ANOVA, p < 0.05; Table 4: F=16.922, p=0.000). Teacher experience effect not significant (ANOVA, p > 0.05; Table 5: p=0.118).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2009 reading comprehension text data (summary task) in Spain, the study compared teacher-rated style scores between ChatGPT and real student summaries and examined differences by teacher gender, age, and experience, finding that ChatGPT received higher style scores than students (all differences > 3 points) and that the ChatGPT9student style gap varied significantly by teacher age but not by teacher gender or experience. This indicates that integrating generative AI into writing/summarizing tasks may produce consistently higher stylistic outputs, but teacher characteristics (especially age) can influence how strongly such differences are perceived in assessment practice.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2009 reading comprehension text (summary task), Spain (secondary students, 149e16)
main_findings.performance_metrics: No ML metrics reported. Descriptive differences: content differences > 2.5 points. Inferential tests: gender effect significant (t-test, p < 0.05; Table 3: p=0.019). Teacher age effect significant (ANOVA, p < 0.05; Table 4: F=6.724, p=0.004). Teacher experience effect not significant (ANOVA, p > 0.05; Table 5: p=0.662).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2009 reading comprehension text data (summary task) in Spain, the study compared teacher-rated content scores between ChatGPT and real student summaries and examined differences by teacher gender, age, and experience, finding that ChatGPT received higher content scores than students (differences > 2.5 points) and that the ChatGPT9student content gap varied significantly by teacher gender and teacher age but not by teacher experience. This indicates that generative AI may outperform students on rubric-based content quality in this task, and that assessment outcomes may be sensitive to teacher demographics, implying the need for calibration and rubric training when AI-generated work is possible.

data.outcome_summary: This study used a PISA 2009 reading comprehension text (385 words) as the source for a classroom summary task administered to 30 Spanish secondary students (149e16) and compared their teacher-rated summaries with a ChatGPT-generated summary camouflaged among student work. Thirty Spanish language teachers (selected across five regions) scored each summary using a rubric with two dimensions: content and style. The results show that ChatGPT obtained higher ratings than students in both dimensions: style differences were all above 3 points and content differences were above 2.5 points. Gender and teacher age significantly moderated the ChatGPT9student gaps (content: gender p=0.019; age p=0.004; style: age p=0.000), while teacher experience did not. No machine-learning model was trained; therefore, findings are about human assessment differences rather than predictive performance, and missing-data handling is not fully documented.
